It explicitly models data distributions, promotes disentangled representations, and aligns with standard regularizers like Batch Norm. Built on a teacher-student setup, the method expands the student’s forward and backward passes onto the teacher’s computational graph. This approach avoids restrictive assumptions—such as Gaussian inputs or independent activations—enabling more grounded theoretical exploration of practical concerns like overfitting, generalization, and feature disentanglement in deep networks.

input:
We present a Neural Program Search, an algorithm to generate programs from
natural language description and a small number of input/output examples. The
algorithm combines methods from Deep Learning and Program Synthesis fields by
designing rich domain-specific language (DSL) and defining efficient search
algorithm guided by a Seq2Tree model on it. To evaluate the quality of the
approach we also present a semi-synthetic dataset of descriptions with test
examples and corresponding programs. We show that our algorithm significantly
outperforms a sequence-to-sequence model with attention baseline.
Improve this in GPT way: We introduce Neural Program Search, a method for generating programs from natural language descriptions and a few input/output examples. It integrates deep learning with program synthesis by employing a rich domain-specific language (DSL) and a guided search algorithm based on a Seq2Tree model. For evaluation, we provide a semi-synthetic dataset of descriptions, tests, and programs. Our approach substantially outperforms a standard sequence-to-sequence model with attention.

input:
Most state-of-the-art neural machine translation systems, despite being
different in architectural skeletons (e.g. recurrence, convolutional), share an
indispensable feature: the Attention. However, most existing attention methods
are token-based and ignore the importance of phrasal alignments, the key
ingredient for the success of phrase-based statistical machine translation. In
this paper, we propose novel phrase-based attention methods to model n-grams of
tokens as attention entities. We incorporate our phrase-based attentions into
the recently proposed Transformer network, and demonstrate that our approach
yields improvements of 1.3 BLEU for English-to-German and 0.5 BLEU for
German-to-English translation tasks on WMT newstest2014 using WMT'16 training
data.
Improve this in GPT way: While most advanced neural machine translation models rely on token-based attention, they overlook the proven value of phrasal alignments from earlier statistical methods. To address this, we introduce novel phrase-based attention mechanisms that treat n-grams as fundamental units. By integrating these into the Transformer architecture, our approach achieves consistent improvements, including gains of 1.3 BLEU for English-to-German and 0.5 BLEU for German-to-English translation on the WMT newstest2014 benchmark.

input:
We introduce the problem of learning distributed representations of edits. By
combining a "neural editor" with an "edit encoder", our models learn to
represent the salient information of an edit and can be used to apply edits to
new inputs. We experiment on natural language and source code edit data. Our
evaluation yields promising results that suggest that our neural network models
learn to capture the structure and semantics of edits. We hope that this
interesting task and data source will inspire other researchers to work further
on this problem.
Improve this in GPT way: We propose the problem of learning distributed representations of edits. Our approach pairs a “neural editor” with an “edit encoder” to capture an edit’s essential information, enabling the application of learned edits to new inputs. Evaluated on natural language and source code, our models show promising ability to learn edit structure and semantics. We present this as a novel task and data source to encourage further research in this direction.

input:
We propose a single neural probabilistic model based on variational
autoencoder that can be conditioned on an arbitrary subset of observed features
and then sample the remaining features in "one shot". The features may be both
real-valued and categorical. Training of the model is performed by stochastic
variational Bayes. The experimental evaluation on synthetic data, as well as
feature imputation and image inpainting problems, shows the effectiveness of
the proposed approach and diversity of the generated samples.
Improve this in GPT way: We introduce a neural probabilistic model based on a conditional variational autoencoder. It can be conditioned on any subset of observed features—real-valued or categorical—and generate the remaining features in a single pass. Training uses stochastic variational inference. Experiments on synthetic data, feature imputation, and image inpainting demonstrate the method’s effectiveness and the diversity of its generated samples.

input:
Understanding and characterizing the subspaces of adversarial examples aid in
studying the robustness of deep neural networks (DNNs) to adversarial
perturbations. Very recently, Ma et al. (ICLR 2018) proposed to use local
intrinsic dimensionality (LID) in layer-wise hidden representations of DNNs to
study adversarial subspaces. It was demonstrated that LID can be used to
characterize the adversarial subspaces associated with different attack
methods, e.g., the Carlini and Wagner's (C&W) attack and the fast gradient sign
attack.
  In this paper, we use MNIST and CIFAR-10 to conduct two new sets of
experiments that are absent in existing LID analysis and report the limitation
of LID in characterizing the corresponding adversarial subspaces, which are (i)
oblivious attacks and LID analysis using adversarial examples with different
confidence levels; and (ii) black-box transfer attacks. For (i), we find that
the performance of LID is very sensitive to the confidence parameter deployed
by an attack, and the LID learned from ensembles of adversarial examples with
varying confidence levels surprisingly gives poor performance. For (ii), we
find that when adversarial examples are crafted from another DNN model, LID is
ineffective in characterizing their adversarial subspaces. These two findings
together suggest the limited capability of LID in characterizing the subspaces
of adversarial examples.
Improve this in GPT way:
Understanding and characterizing the subspaces of adversarial examples aids in studying the robustness of deep neural networks (DNNs). Recently, Ma et al. (ICLR 2018) proposed using local intrinsic dimensionality (LID) in the hidden representations of DNNs to analyze these adversarial subspaces. Their work demonstrated that LID could characterize subspaces produced by specific attacks, such as the Carlini and Wagner (C&W) attack and the fast gradient sign method.

In this paper, we extend the LID analysis through two new sets of experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10, addressing gaps in the existing literature. First, we examine oblivious attacks and analyze adversarial examples generated with varying confidence levels. Our results show that LID performance is highly sensitive to the attack’s confidence parameter; moreover, learning LID from ensembles of examples with mixed confidence levels yields surprisingly poor results. Second, we evaluate black-box transfer attacks, where adversarial examples are crafted using a different DNN model. Here, LID proves ineffective in characterizing the resulting adversarial subspaces.

Together, these findings reveal significant limitations in the ability of LID to characterize adversarial subspaces, suggesting that its applicability may be narrower than previously indicated.

input:
Generative adversarial networks (GANs) form a generative modeling approach
known for producing appealing samples, but they are notably difficult to train.
One common way to tackle this issue has been to propose new formulations of the
GAN objective. Yet, surprisingly few studies have looked at optimization
methods designed for this adversarial training. In this work, we cast GAN
optimization problems in the general variational inequality framework. Tapping
into the mathematical programming literature, we counter some common
misconceptions about the difficulties of saddle point optimization and propose
to extend techniques designed for variational inequalities to the training of
GANs. We apply averaging, extrapolation and a computationally cheaper variant
that we call extrapolation from the past to the stochastic gradient method
(SGD) and Adam.
Improve this in GPT way: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) are a powerful generative modeling approach, celebrated for their ability to produce high-quality samples, yet they remain notoriously challenging to train. While much research has focused on developing new objective functions, surprisingly little attention has been paid to the optimization methods used for this adversarial training. In this work, we reframe GAN optimization within the general variational inequality framework. Drawing on established mathematical programming literature, we address common misconceptions about saddle point optimization and propose adapting techniques designed for variational inequalities to GAN training. Specifically, we extend stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and Adam with averaging, extrapolation, and a more efficient variant we term *extrapolation from the past*.

input:
Neural message passing algorithms for semi-supervised classification on
graphs have recently achieved great success. However, for classifying a node
these methods only consider nodes that are a few propagation steps away and the
size of this utilized neighborhood is hard to extend. In this paper, we use the
relationship between graph convolutional networks (GCN) and PageRank to derive
an improved propagation scheme based on personalized PageRank. We utilize this
propagation procedure to construct a simple model, personalized propagation of
neural predictions (PPNP), and its fast approximation, APPNP. Our model's
training time is on par or faster and its number of parameters on par or lower
than previous models. It leverages a large, adjustable neighborhood for
classification and can be easily combined with any neural network. We show that
this model outperforms several recently proposed methods for semi-supervised
classification in the most thorough study done so far for GCN-like models. Our
implementation is available online.
Improve this in GPT way:
Recent advances in graph neural networks have achieved strong results in semi-supervised node classification. However, existing methods, such as graph convolutional networks (GCNs), are inherently limited to aggregating information from only a few neighboring steps, making it difficult to leverage larger, more informative neighborhoods.

In this work, we bridge GCNs and PageRank to develop an enhanced propagation scheme based on personalized PageRank. This leads to a straightforward model: Personalized Propagation of Neural Predictions (PPNP), along with its fast approximation, APPNP. Our approach maintains competitive training times and parameter counts while enabling adjustable, large-scale neighborhood aggregation. It can be seamlessly integrated with any neural network.

In the most comprehensive study of GCN-type models to date, we demonstrate that PPNP and APPNP consistently outperform recent semi-supervised methods. Code is publicly available.

input:
We identify obfuscated gradients, a kind of gradient masking, as a phenomenon
that leads to a false sense of security in defenses against adversarial
examples. While defenses that cause obfuscated gradients appear to defeat
iterative optimization-based attacks, we find defenses relying on this effect
can be circumvented. We describe characteristic behaviors of defenses
exhibiting the effect, and for each of the three types of obfuscated gradients
we discover, we develop attack techniques to overcome it. In a case study,
examining non-certified white-box-secure defenses at ICLR 2018, we find
obfuscated gradients are a common occurrence, with 7 of 9 defenses relying on
obfuscated gradients. Our new attacks successfully circumvent 6 completely, and
1 partially, in the original threat model each paper considers.
Improve this in GPT way:
We identify obfuscated gradients—a form of gradient masking—as a phenomenon that creates a misleading sense of security in adversarial defenses. Although such defenses can appear robust against iterative optimization attacks, we demonstrate they are often vulnerable to circumvention. We outline the characteristic behaviors of these defenses and, for each of the three obfuscated gradient types we uncover, develop tailored attacks to defeat them. In a case study of non-certified white-box defenses from ICLR 2018, we find obfuscated gradients are prevalent: 7 of 9 defenses rely on this effect. Our novel attacks completely break 6 of these defenses and partially break 1, all within each paper’s original threat model.

(Word count: 121)

input:
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have become the method of choice for
learning problems involving 2D planar images. However, a number of problems of
recent interest have created a demand for models that can analyze spherical
images. Examples include omnidirectional vision for drones, robots, and
autonomous cars, molecular regression problems, and global weather and climate
modelling. A naive application of convolutional networks to a planar projection
of the spherical signal is destined to fail, because the space-varying
distortions introduced by such a projection will make translational weight
sharing ineffective.
  In this paper we introduce the building blocks for constructing spherical
CNNs. We propose a definition for the spherical cross-correlation that is both
expressive and rotation-equivariant. The spherical correlation satisfies a
generalized Fourier theorem, which allows us to compute it efficiently using a
generalized (non-commutative) Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) algorithm. We
demonstrate the computational efficiency, numerical accuracy, and effectiveness
of spherical CNNs applied to 3D model recognition and atomization energy
regression.
Improve this in GPT way:
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are the established standard for processing conventional 2D images. Yet, emerging challenges increasingly require models capable of interpreting spherical imagery. Key applications span omnidirectional vision for autonomous vehicles, drones, and robotics, along with molecular property regression and global climate modeling. Simply applying planar CNNs to a flattened projection of spherical data is inherently flawed, as the resulting spatial distortions undermine the fundamental translational weight-sharing principle of convolutions.

This paper presents the essential components for building effective spherical CNNs. We define a spherical cross-correlation that is both highly expressive and equivariant to rotations. This operation adheres to a generalized Fourier theorem, enabling efficient computation via a non-commutative Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) algorithm. We validate our approach by demonstrating its computational efficiency, numerical accuracy, and strong performance on tasks including 3D object recognition and atomization energy regression.

(Word count: 159)

input:
The inclusion of Computer Vision and Deep Learning technologies in
Agriculture aims to increase the harvest quality, and productivity of farmers.
During postharvest, the export market and quality evaluation are affected by
assorting of fruits and vegetables. In particular, apples are susceptible to a
wide range of defects that can occur during harvesting or/and during the
post-harvesting period. This paper aims to help farmers with post-harvest
handling by exploring if recent computer vision and deep learning methods such
as the YOLOv3 (Redmon & Farhadi (2018)) can help in detecting healthy apples
from apples with defects.
Improve this in GPT way:
Integrating Computer Vision and Deep Learning into agriculture enhances harvest quality and farmer productivity. Postharvest processes, especially fruit and vegetable sorting, critically impact export markets and quality assessment. Apples are particularly prone to defects from harvesting and postharvest handling. This study investigates whether modern methods like YOLOv3 (Redmon & Farhadi, 2018) can effectively distinguish healthy apples from defective ones, thereby aiding farmers in postharvest management.

(Word count: 95)

input:
In this work, we analyze the reinstatement mechanism introduced by Ritter et
al. (2018) to reveal two classes of neurons that emerge in the agent's working
memory (an epLSTM cell) when trained using episodic meta-RL on an episodic
variant of the Harlow visual fixation task. Specifically, Abstract neurons
encode knowledge shared across tasks, while Episodic neurons carry information
relevant for a specific episode's task.
Improve this in GPT way: This study examines the reinstatement mechanism from Ritter et al. (2018). We identify two distinct neuron classes that arise in an agent's working memory (an epLSTM) during episodic meta-RL training on a variant of the Harlow task. Abstract neurons encode knowledge common across tasks, whereas Episodic neurons hold information specific to a single episode's goal.

input:
The rate-distortion-perception function (RDPF; Blau and Michaeli, 2019) has
emerged as a useful tool for thinking about realism and distortion of
reconstructions in lossy compression. Unlike the rate-distortion function,
however, it is unknown whether encoders and decoders exist that achieve the
rate suggested by the RDPF. Building on results by Li and El Gamal (2018), we
show that the RDPF can indeed be achieved using stochastic, variable-length
codes. For this class of codes, we also prove that the RDPF lower-bounds the
achievable rate
Improve this in GPT way: The rate-distortion-perception function (RDPF) is a valuable framework for analyzing realism and distortion in lossy compression. However, unlike the classic rate-distortion function, it has been unclear whether practical encoders and decoders can achieve the rates it suggests. By extending prior work by Li and El Gamal, we demonstrate that the RDPF is achievable using stochastic, variable-length codes. For this class of codes, we further prove that the RDPF provides a lower bound on the achievable rate.

input:
It is by now well-known that small adversarial perturbations can induce
classification errors in deep neural networks (DNNs). In this paper, we make
the case that sparse representations of the input data are a crucial tool for
combating such attacks. For linear classifiers, we show that a sparsifying
front end is provably effective against $\ell_{\infty}$-bounded attacks,
reducing output distortion due to the attack by a factor of roughly $K / N$
where $N$ is the data dimension and $K$ is the sparsity level. We then extend
this concept to DNNs, showing that a "locally linear" model can be used to
develop a theoretical foundation for crafting attacks and defenses.
Experimental results for the MNIST dataset show the efficacy of the proposed
sparsifying front end.
Improve this in GPT way:
It is well-established that small adversarial perturbations can cause deep neural networks (DNNs) to misclassify inputs. This paper argues that sparse data representations are a vital defense mechanism. For linear classifiers, we prove that a sparsifying front end robustly mitigates $\ell_{\infty}$-bounded attacks, reducing the attack-induced output distortion by approximately a factor of $K/N$. Here, $N$ is the data dimension and $K$ is the sparsity level. We generalize this approach to DNNs using a "locally linear" model, providing a theoretical basis for both designing attacks and constructing defenses. Experiments on MNIST confirm the effectiveness of the proposed sparsifying front end.

(Word count: 124)

input:
We propose a new sample-efficient methodology, called Supervised Policy
Update (SPU), for deep reinforcement learning. Starting with data generated by
the current policy, SPU formulates and solves a constrained optimization
problem in the non-parameterized proximal policy space. Using supervised
regression, it then converts the optimal non-parameterized policy to a
parameterized policy, from which it draws new samples. The methodology is
general in that it applies to both discrete and continuous action spaces, and
can handle a wide variety of proximity constraints for the non-parameterized
optimization problem. We show how the Natural Policy Gradient and Trust Region
Policy Optimization (NPG/TRPO) problems, and the Proximal Policy Optimization
(PPO) problem can be addressed by this methodology. The SPU implementation is
much simpler than TRPO. In terms of sample efficiency, our extensive
experiments show SPU outperforms TRPO in Mujoco simulated robotic tasks and
outperforms PPO in Atari video game tasks.
Improve this in GPT way: We introduce Supervised Policy Update (SPU), a sample-efficient methodology for deep reinforcement learning. SPU begins with data from the current policy and solves a constrained optimization within a non-parameterized proximal policy space. The resulting optimal policy is then converted into a parameterized form via supervised regression, enabling new sample collection. This general approach works for both discrete and continuous actions and accommodates diverse proximity constraints. We demonstrate that SPU can address the problems of Natural Policy Gradient, Trust Region Policy Optimization (NPG/TRPO), and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). Notably, SPU is simpler to implement than TRPO. In extensive testing, SPU achieves superior sample efficiency, outperforming TRPO on Mujoco robotic simulations and surpassing PPO in Atari game tasks.

input:
We present a parameterized synthetic dataset called Moving Symbols to support
the objective study of video prediction networks. Using several instantiations
of the dataset in which variation is explicitly controlled, we highlight issues
in an existing state-of-the-art approach and propose the use of a performance
metric with greater semantic meaning to improve experimental interpretability.
Our dataset provides canonical test cases that will help the community better
understand, and eventually improve, the representations learned by such
networks in the future. Code is available at
https://github.com/rszeto/moving-symbols .
Improve this in GPT way: We introduce Moving Symbols, a parameterized synthetic dataset designed for the objective evaluation of video prediction networks. By explicitly controlling variations across dataset versions, we uncover limitations in a leading existing method and advocate for a more semantically meaningful performance metric to enhance interpretability. This dataset offers canonical test cases to help the community better understand—and ultimately improve—the representations learned by these networks. Code: https://github.com/rszeto/moving-symbols.

input:
This work is a part of ICLR Reproducibility Challenge 2019, we try to
reproduce the results in the conference submission PADAM: Closing The
Generalization Gap of Adaptive Gradient Methods In Training Deep Neural
Networks. Adaptive gradient methods proposed in past demonstrate a degraded
generalization performance than the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with
momentum. The authors try to address this problem by designing a new
optimization algorithm that bridges the gap between the space of Adaptive
Gradient algorithms and SGD with momentum. With this method a new tunable
hyperparameter called partially adaptive parameter p is introduced that varies
between [0, 0.5]. We build the proposed optimizer and use it to mirror the
experiments performed by the authors. We review and comment on the empirical
analysis performed by the authors. Finally, we also propose a future direction
for further study of Padam. Our code is available at:
https://github.com/yashkant/Padam-Tensorflow
Improve this in GPT way:
This study was conducted as part of the ICLR 2019 Reproducibility Challenge, focusing on the paper “PADAM: Closing The Generalization Gap of Adaptive Gradient Methods In Training Deep Neural Networks.” Prior adaptive gradient methods often exhibit poorer generalization compared to Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) with momentum. The authors address this by introducing PADAM, a novel optimizer that bridges the gap between adaptive methods and SGD. A key innovation is the partially adaptive parameter *p*, tunable between 0 and 0.5. We implemented this optimizer and replicated the original experiments. Our work reviews the authors’ empirical analysis, provides commentary, and suggests a direction for future research on PADAM. The code is available at: https://github.com/yashkant/Padam-Tensorflow.

(Word count: 146)

input:
We present a large-scale empirical study of catastrophic forgetting (CF) in
modern Deep Neural Network (DNN) models that perform sequential (or:
incremental) learning. A new experimental protocol is proposed that enforces
typical constraints encountered in application scenarios. As the investigation
is empirical, we evaluate CF behavior on the hitherto largest number of visual
classification datasets, from each of which we construct a representative
number of Sequential Learning Tasks (SLTs) in close alignment to previous works
on CF. Our results clearly indicate that there is no model that avoids CF for
all investigated datasets and SLTs under application conditions. We conclude
with a discussion of potential solutions and workarounds to CF, notably for the
EWC and IMM models.
Improve this in GPT way: We present a comprehensive empirical analysis of catastrophic forgetting (CF) in modern Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) engaged in sequential learning. A novel experimental protocol is introduced, designed to reflect realistic application constraints. This study evaluates CF across the largest collection of visual classification datasets to date, generating a representative set of Sequential Learning Tasks (SLTs) consistent with prior research. Findings demonstrate that no examined model consistently avoids CF across all datasets and SLTs under practical conditions. The discussion concludes by exploring potential remedies and workarounds for CF, with particular attention to Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) and Incremental Moment Matching (IMM) models.

input:
Deep learning models for graphs have advanced the state of the art on many
tasks. Despite their recent success, little is known about their robustness. We
investigate training time attacks on graph neural networks for node
classification that perturb the discrete graph structure. Our core principle is
to use meta-gradients to solve the bilevel problem underlying training-time
attacks, essentially treating the graph as a hyperparameter to optimize. Our
experiments show that small graph perturbations consistently lead to a strong
decrease in performance for graph convolutional networks, and even transfer to
unsupervised embeddings. Remarkably, the perturbations created by our algorithm
can misguide the graph neural networks such that they perform worse than a
simple baseline that ignores all relational information. Our attacks do not
assume any knowledge about or access to the target classifiers.
Improve this in GPT way: Recent advances in deep learning for graphs have significantly improved performance across numerous tasks. However, the robustness of these models remains largely unexplored. In this work, we examine training-time attacks against graph neural networks (GNNs) for node classification, focusing on perturbations to the discrete graph structure. Our key innovation is to employ meta-gradients to address the underlying bilevel optimization problem, effectively treating the graph itself as a learnable hyperparameter. Experiments reveal that even minor structural perturbations can cause a substantial performance drop in graph convolutional networks, with effects transferring to unsupervised embeddings. Notably, our method can mislead GNNs to underperform a simple baseline that disregards all relational information. These attacks require no prior knowledge of or access to the target classifiers.

input:
Multi-domain learning (MDL) aims at obtaining a model with minimal average
risk across multiple domains. Our empirical motivation is automated microscopy
data, where cultured cells are imaged after being exposed to known and unknown
chemical perturbations, and each dataset displays significant experimental
bias. This paper presents a multi-domain adversarial learning approach, MuLANN,
to leverage multiple datasets with overlapping but distinct class sets, in a
semi-supervised setting. Our contributions include: i) a bound on the average-
and worst-domain risk in MDL, obtained using the H-divergence; ii) a new loss
to accommodate semi-supervised multi-domain learning and domain adaptation;
iii) the experimental validation of the approach, improving on the state of the
art on two standard image benchmarks, and a novel bioimage dataset, Cell.
Improve this in GPT way: Multi-domain learning (MDL) seeks a model that minimizes average risk across multiple domains. Our work is driven by automated microscopy data, where cultured cells are imaged under known and unknown chemical perturbations, with each dataset exhibiting substantial experimental bias. We introduce MuLANN, a multi-domain adversarial learning method designed for semi-supervised settings with overlapping but distinct class sets. Our contributions are threefold: i) a bound on average- and worst-domain risk in MDL derived via H-divergence; ii) a novel loss function for semi-supervised multi-domain learning and adaptation; iii) experimental validation showing state-of-the-art improvements on two standard image benchmarks and a new bioimage dataset, Cell.

input:
We propose a neural network for unsupervised anomaly detection with a novel
robust subspace recovery layer (RSR layer). This layer seeks to extract the
underlying subspace from a latent representation of the given data and removes
outliers that lie away from this subspace. It is used within an autoencoder.
The encoder maps the data into a latent space, from which the RSR layer
extracts the subspace. The decoder then smoothly maps back the underlying
subspace to a "manifold" close to the original inliers. Inliers and outliers
are distinguished according to the distances between the original and mapped
positions (small for inliers and large for outliers). Extensive numerical
experiments with both image and document datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art
precision and recall.
Improve this in GPT way: We introduce a neural network for unsupervised anomaly detection, featuring a novel robust subspace recovery (RSR) layer. Integrated within an autoencoder, this layer extracts the principal subspace from a latent representation while filtering out outliers that deviate from it. The encoder first projects data into the latent space, where the RSR layer isolates the underlying subspace. The decoder then smoothly reconstructs this subspace, producing a manifold near the original inliers. Anomalies are identified by measuring the reconstruction distance—small for inliers, large for outliers. Extensive experiments on image and document datasets achieve state-of-the-art precision and recall.

input:
We propose a novel node embedding of directed graphs to statistical
manifolds, which is based on a global minimization of pairwise relative entropy
and graph geodesics in a non-linear way. Each node is encoded with a
probability density function over a measurable space. Furthermore, we analyze
the connection between the geometrical properties of such embedding and their
efficient learning procedure. Extensive experiments show that our proposed
embedding is better in preserving the global geodesic information of graphs, as
well as outperforming existing embedding models on directed graphs in a variety
of evaluation metrics, in an unsupervised setting.
Improve this in GPT way: We introduce a novel method for embedding directed graphs onto statistical manifolds. This approach minimizes pairwise relative entropy while incorporating graph geodesics in a non-linear, global optimization. Each node is represented by a probability density function. We also examine the relationship between the geometric properties of the embedding and its efficient learning process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our model better preserves global geodesic information and outperforms existing unsupervised embeddings for directed graphs across multiple evaluation metrics.

input:
The impressive lifelong learning in animal brains is primarily enabled by
plastic changes in synaptic connectivity. Importantly, these changes are not
passive, but are actively controlled by neuromodulation, which is itself under
the control of the brain. The resulting self-modifying abilities of the brain
play an important role in learning and adaptation, and are a major basis for
biological reinforcement learning. Here we show for the first time that
artificial neural networks with such neuromodulated plasticity can be trained
with gradient descent. Extending previous work on differentiable Hebbian
plasticity, we propose a differentiable formulation for the neuromodulation of
plasticity. We show that neuromodulated plasticity improves the performance of
neural networks on both reinforcement learning and supervised learning tasks.
In one task, neuromodulated plastic LSTMs with millions of parameters
outperform standard LSTMs on a benchmark language modeling task (controlling
for the number of parameters). We conclude that differentiable neuromodulation
of plasticity offers a powerful new framework for training neural networks.
Improve this in GPT way:
The remarkable lifelong learning capacity of animal brains is fundamentally driven by plastic changes in synaptic connections. Crucially, this plasticity is not passive; it is actively regulated by neuromodulation, a process itself directed by the brain. This capacity for self-modification is central to learning, adaptation, and serves as a core mechanism for biological reinforcement learning.

We demonstrate, for the first time, that artificial neural networks featuring this neuromodulated plasticity can be successfully trained using gradient descent. Building on prior research into differentiable Hebbian plasticity, we introduce a novel, differentiable formulation for neuromodulating plasticity itself. Our results show that networks with neuromodulated plasticity achieve superior performance in both reinforcement and supervised learning. For instance, on a benchmark language modeling task, neuromodulated plastic LSTMs with millions of parameters outperform standard LSTMs of comparable size.

We conclude that differentiable neuromodulation of plasticity provides a powerful and innovative framework for training neural networks.

input:
Euclidean geometry has historically been the typical "workhorse" for machine
learning applications due to its power and simplicity. However, it has recently
been shown that geometric spaces with constant non-zero curvature improve
representations and performance on a variety of data types and downstream
tasks. Consequently, generative models like Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
have been successfully generalized to elliptical and hyperbolic latent spaces.
While these approaches work well on data with particular kinds of biases e.g.
tree-like data for a hyperbolic VAE, there exists no generic approach unifying
and leveraging all three models. We develop a Mixed-curvature Variational
Autoencoder, an efficient way to train a VAE whose latent space is a product of
constant curvature Riemannian manifolds, where the per-component curvature is
fixed or learnable. This generalizes the Euclidean VAE to curved latent spaces
and recovers it when curvatures of all latent space components go to 0.
Improve this in GPT way: Euclidean geometry has long served as machine learning's foundational framework, prized for its power and simplicity. Recent advances, however, demonstrate that geometric spaces with constant non-zero curvature—specifically elliptical and hyperbolic—can enhance data representations and boost performance across diverse data types and tasks. This has led to successful generalizations of models like Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) into these curved spaces. Yet, current approaches remain specialized; for instance, hyperbolic VAEs excel with tree-like data, but a unified model encompassing all three geometries is absent. We introduce the Mixed-curvature Variational Autoencoder, which efficiently trains a VAE using a latent space composed of constant-curvature Riemannian manifolds. Individual curvatures can be fixed or learned, offering a broad framework that includes the Euclidean VAE as a special case when all curvatures approach zero.

input:
We explore various methods for computing sentence representations from
pre-trained word embeddings without any training, i.e., using nothing but
random parameterizations. Our aim is to put sentence embeddings on more solid
footing by 1) looking at how much modern sentence embeddings gain over random
methods---as it turns out, surprisingly little; and by 2) providing the field
with more appropriate baselines going forward---which are, as it turns out,
quite strong. We also make important observations about proper experimental
protocol for sentence classification evaluation, together with recommendations
for future research.
Improve this in GPT way: We investigate methods for deriving sentence representations directly from pre-trained word embeddings, using only random parameterizations and no training. Our goal is to establish a stronger foundation for sentence embeddings by demonstrating that modern techniques yield surprisingly minimal gains over these random baselines, which themselves prove to be quite robust. Additionally, we offer critical insights on experimental design for sentence classification and provide recommendations for future work.

input:
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are one of the most popular tools for
learning complex high dimensional distributions. However, generalization
properties of GANs have not been well understood. In this paper, we analyze the
generalization of GANs in practical settings. We show that discriminators
trained on discrete datasets with the original GAN loss have poor
generalization capability and do not approximate the theoretically optimal
discriminator. We propose a zero-centered gradient penalty for improving the
generalization of the discriminator by pushing it toward the optimal
discriminator. The penalty guarantees the generalization and convergence of
GANs. Experiments on synthetic and large scale datasets verify our theoretical
analysis.
Improve this in GPT way: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are a leading method for modeling complex data distributions, yet their generalization behavior remains poorly characterized. This work provides a practical analysis of GAN generalization. We demonstrate that discriminators trained with the standard loss on finite datasets generalize poorly and deviate from the theoretically optimal function. To address this, we introduce a zero-centered gradient penalty that steers the discriminator toward optimality. This penalty formally ensures both improved generalization and training convergence. Our theoretical claims are validated through experiments on both synthetic and large-scale real-world datasets.

input:
In this paper we propose to perform model ensembling in a multiclass or a
multilabel learning setting using Wasserstein (W.) barycenters. Optimal
transport metrics, such as the Wasserstein distance, allow incorporating
semantic side information such as word embeddings. Using W. barycenters to find
the consensus between models allows us to balance confidence and semantics in
finding the agreement between the models. We show applications of Wasserstein
ensembling in attribute-based classification, multilabel learning and image
captioning generation. These results show that the W. ensembling is a viable
alternative to the basic geometric or arithmetic mean ensembling.
Improve this in GPT way: This paper introduces a method for model ensembling in multiclass and multilabel learning using Wasserstein barycenters. By leveraging optimal transport metrics, the approach incorporates semantic side information, such as word embeddings, to balance model confidence with semantic meaning when finding consensus. We demonstrate applications in attribute-based classification, multilabel learning, and image captioning. Results indicate that Wasserstein ensembling serves as a viable alternative to traditional geometric or arithmetic mean ensembling techniques.

input:
We present a method that learns to integrate temporal information, from a
learned dynamics model, with ambiguous visual information, from a learned
vision model, in the context of interacting agents. Our method is based on a
graph-structured variational recurrent neural network (Graph-VRNN), which is
trained end-to-end to infer the current state of the (partially observed)
world, as well as to forecast future states. We show that our method
outperforms various baselines on two sports datasets, one based on real
basketball trajectories, and one generated by a soccer game engine.
Improve this in GPT way: We introduce a method that fuses ambiguous visual data from a learned vision model with temporal dynamics from a learned dynamics model, specifically for multi-agent interactions. This is achieved using a graph-structured variational recurrent neural network (Graph-VRNN), trained end-to-end to infer the current state of a partially observed world and to predict future states. Our approach demonstrates superior performance against multiple baselines on two sports datasets: real basketball trajectories and simulated soccer data from a game engine.

input:
Modern neural networks are over-parametrized. In particular, each rectified
linear hidden unit can be modified by a multiplicative factor by adjusting
input and output weights, without changing the rest of the network. Inspired by
the Sinkhorn-Knopp algorithm, we introduce a fast iterative method for
minimizing the L2 norm of the weights, equivalently the weight decay
regularizer. It provably converges to a unique solution. Interleaving our
algorithm with SGD during training improves the test accuracy. For small
batches, our approach offers an alternative to batch-and group-normalization on
CIFAR-10 and ImageNet with a ResNet-18.
Improve this in GPT way:
Modern neural networks are highly over-parametrized. For instance, each ReLU unit can be scaled by adjusting its incoming and outgoing weights without affecting overall network behavior. Drawing inspiration from the Sinkhorn-Knopp algorithm, we propose a fast iterative method to minimize the L2 norm of the weights—equivalent to weight decay. The algorithm provably converges to a unique solution. When interleaved with SGD, it boosts test accuracy. On CIFAR-10 and ImageNet using ResNet-18, our method provides an effective alternative to batch and group normalization, especially for small batch sizes.

Word count: 100

input:
We present graph wavelet neural network (GWNN), a novel graph convolutional
neural network (CNN), leveraging graph wavelet transform to address the
shortcomings of previous spectral graph CNN methods that depend on graph
Fourier transform. Different from graph Fourier transform, graph wavelet
transform can be obtained via a fast algorithm without requiring matrix
eigendecomposition with high computational cost. Moreover, graph wavelets are
sparse and localized in vertex domain, offering high efficiency and good
interpretability for graph convolution. The proposed GWNN significantly
outperforms previous spectral graph CNNs in the task of graph-based
semi-supervised classification on three benchmark datasets: Cora, Citeseer and
Pubmed.
Improve this in GPT way: We introduce the Graph Wavelet Neural Network (GWNN), a new spectral graph convolutional network that replaces the graph Fourier transform with a graph wavelet transform. This approach overcomes key limitations of prior methods by eliminating the need for computationally expensive matrix eigendecomposition. Furthermore, graph wavelets are sparse and localized in the vertex domain, leading to more efficient and interpretable graph convolutions. Our experiments demonstrate that GWNN substantially outperforms existing spectral graph CNNs in semi-supervised classification on the Cora, Citeseer, and Pubmed datasets.

input:
We present the perceptor gradients algorithm -- a novel approach to learning
symbolic representations based on the idea of decomposing an agent's policy
into i) a perceptor network extracting symbols from raw observation data and
ii) a task encoding program which maps the input symbols to output actions. We
show that the proposed algorithm is able to learn representations that can be
directly fed into a Linear-Quadratic Regulator (LQR) or a general purpose A*
planner. Our experimental results confirm that the perceptor gradients
algorithm is able to efficiently learn transferable symbolic representations as
well as generate new observations according to a semantically meaningful
specification.
Improve this in GPT way: We introduce the perceptor gradients algorithm, a novel method for learning symbolic representations. It decomposes an agent's policy into two components: a perceptor network that extracts symbols from raw observations, and a task program that maps these symbols to actions. We demonstrate that the learned representations can be directly utilized by a Linear-Quadratic Regulator (LQR) or a general-purpose A* planner. Experimental results confirm the algorithm efficiently acquires transferable symbolic representations and can generate new observations based on semantically meaningful specifications.

input:
We study the robustness to symmetric label noise of GNNs training procedures.
By combining the nonlinear neural message-passing models (e.g. Graph
Isomorphism Networks, GraphSAGE, etc.) with loss correction methods, we present
a noise-tolerant approach for the graph classification task. Our experiments
show that test accuracy can be improved under the artificial symmetric noisy
setting.
Improve this in GPT way: We investigate the robustness of Graph Neural Network (GNN) training to symmetric label noise. By integrating nonlinear message-passing architectures with loss correction techniques, we propose a noise-tolerant method for graph classification. Experiments demonstrate that this approach improves test accuracy under artificially generated symmetric label noise.

input:
The recent use of `Big Code' with state-of-the-art deep learning methods
offers promising avenues to ease program source code writing and correction. As
a first step towards automatic code repair, we implemented a graph neural
network model that predicts token types for Javascript programs. The
predictions achieve an accuracy above $90\%$, which improves on previous
similar work.
Improve this in GPT way: The application of "Big Code" with advanced deep learning presents promising opportunities to simplify programming and correction tasks. As an initial step toward automated code repair, we developed a graph neural network model for predicting token types in JavaScript. Our approach achieves over 90% accuracy, surpassing prior similar efforts.

input:
In this paper we consider self-supervised representation learning to improve
sample efficiency in reinforcement learning (RL). We propose a forward
prediction objective for simultaneously learning embeddings of states and
action sequences. These embeddings capture the structure of the environment's
dynamics, enabling efficient policy learning. We demonstrate that our action
embeddings alone improve the sample efficiency and peak performance of
model-free RL on control from low-dimensional states. By combining state and
action embeddings, we achieve efficient learning of high-quality policies on
goal-conditioned continuous control from pixel observations in only 1-2 million
environment steps.
Improve this in GPT way: This paper introduces a self-supervised method to enhance reinforcement learning (RL) sample efficiency. We learn state and action sequence embeddings via a forward prediction objective, which captures environmental dynamics to streamline policy learning. Using only the action embeddings boosts the sample efficiency and peak performance of model-free RL with low-dimensional states. Integrating both state and action embeddings enables learning high-quality, goal-conditioned continuous control policies directly from pixels in just 1-2 million environment steps.

input:
We study the problem of learning permutation invariant representations that
can capture "flexible" notions of containment. We formalize this problem via a
measure theoretic definition of multisets, and obtain a theoretically-motivated
learning model. We propose training this model on a novel task: predicting the
size of the symmetric difference (or intersection) between pairs of multisets.
We demonstrate that our model not only performs very well on predicting
containment relations (and more effectively predicts the sizes of symmetric
differences and intersections than DeepSets-based approaches with unconstrained
object representations), but that it also learns meaningful representations.
Improve this in GPT way: We investigate the problem of learning permutation-invariant representations capable of capturing flexible containment concepts. Using a measure-theoretic definition of multisets, we derive a theoretically-grounded model. This model is trained on a novel task: predicting the size of the symmetric difference or intersection between multiset pairs. Our approach outperforms DeepSets-based methods in predicting both containment relations and set-operation sizes, while also learning semantically meaningful representations.

input:
One way to interpret trained deep neural networks (DNNs) is by inspecting
characteristics that neurons in the model respond to, such as by iteratively
optimising the model input (e.g., an image) to maximally activate specific
neurons. However, this requires a careful selection of hyper-parameters to
generate interpretable examples for each neuron of interest, and current
methods rely on a manual, qualitative evaluation of each setting, which is
prohibitively slow. We introduce a new metric that uses Fr\'echet Inception
Distance (FID) to encourage similarity between model activations for real and
generated data. This provides an efficient way to evaluate a set of generated
examples for each setting of hyper-parameters. We also propose a novel
GAN-based method for generating explanations that enables an efficient search
through the input space and imposes a strong prior favouring realistic outputs.
We apply our approach to a classification model trained to predict whether a
music audio recording contains singing voice. Our results suggest that this
proposed metric successfully selects hyper-parameters leading to interpretable
examples, avoiding the need for manual evaluation. Moreover, we see that
examples synthesised to maximise or minimise the predicted probability of
singing voice presence exhibit vocal or non-vocal characteristics,
respectively, suggesting that our approach is able to generate suitable
explanations for understanding concepts learned by a neural network.
Improve this in GPT way:
A key approach for interpreting trained deep neural networks (DNNs) involves analyzing what activates their neurons, often by optimizing an input—like an image—to maximally stimulate specific neurons. However, this process demands careful hyper-parameter tuning to produce clear, interpretable examples for each neuron, and current techniques rely on slow, manual qualitative assessment. To address this, we introduce a novel metric based on the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) that promotes similarity between model activations for real and generated data. This offers an efficient, automated way to evaluate hyper-parameter settings.

Additionally, we propose a new GAN-based method for generating explanations, which enables efficient exploration of the input space while incorporating a strong prior for realistic outputs. We demonstrate our approach on a classification model trained to detect singing voice in audio recordings. Results indicate that our metric successfully selects hyper-parameters yielding interpretable examples, eliminating the need for manual inspection. Furthermore, examples synthesized to either maximize or minimize the predicted probability of singing voice consistently display vocal or non-vocal traits, respectively. This confirms that our method can generate meaningful explanations for understanding concepts learned by a neural network.

input:
We propose Symplectic Recurrent Neural Networks (SRNNs) as learning
algorithms that capture the dynamics of physical systems from observed
trajectories. An SRNN models the Hamiltonian function of the system by a neural
network and furthermore leverages symplectic integration, multiple-step
training and initial state optimization to address the challenging numerical
issues associated with Hamiltonian systems. We show that SRNNs succeed reliably
on complex and noisy Hamiltonian systems. We also show how to augment the SRNN
integration scheme in order to handle stiff dynamical systems such as bouncing
billiards.
Improve this in GPT way: We introduce Symplectic Recurrent Neural Networks (SRNNs), a novel class of learning algorithms designed to infer the dynamics of physical systems from observed trajectory data. By modeling the system's Hamiltonian with a neural network and employing symplectic integration, multi-step training, and initial state optimization, SRNNs effectively address the numerical challenges inherent in Hamiltonian dynamics. Our results demonstrate that SRNNs reliably learn complex and noisy Hamiltonian systems. Furthermore, we present an augmented integration scheme enabling SRNNs to manage stiff systems, including bouncing billiards.

input:
Spectral embedding is a popular technique for the representation of graph
data. Several regularization techniques have been proposed to improve the
quality of the embedding with respect to downstream tasks like clustering. In
this paper, we explain on a simple block model the impact of the complete graph
regularization, whereby a constant is added to all entries of the adjacency
matrix. Specifically, we show that the regularization forces the spectral
embedding to focus on the largest blocks, making the representation less
sensitive to noise or outliers. We illustrate these results on both on both
synthetic and real data, showing how regularization improves standard
clustering scores.
Improve this in GPT way:
Spectral embedding is a widely used method for representing graph data. Various regularization techniques have been proposed to enhance embedding quality for downstream tasks such as clustering. This paper analyzes, through a simple block model, the effect of complete graph regularization—adding a constant to every entry of the adjacency matrix. We demonstrate that this regularization directs the spectral embedding to emphasize the largest blocks, thereby reducing sensitivity to noise and outliers. These findings are illustrated using both synthetic and real-world data, where regularization consistently improves standard clustering performance.

**Word count:** 104

input:
In this work we study locality and compositionality in the context of
learning representations for Zero Shot Learning (ZSL). In order to well-isolate
the importance of these properties in learned representations, we impose the
additional constraint that, differently from most recent work in ZSL, no
pre-training on different datasets (e.g. ImageNet) is performed. The results of
our experiments show how locality, in terms of small parts of the input, and
compositionality, i.e. how well can the learned representations be expressed as
a function of a smaller vocabulary, are both deeply related to generalization
and motivate the focus on more local-aware models in future research directions
for representation learning.
Improve this in GPT way: In this study, we investigate the roles of locality and compositionality within representation learning for Zero-Shot Learning (ZSL). To clearly isolate the impact of these properties, we introduce a key constraint: unlike most contemporary ZSL approaches, our method does not employ any pre-training on external datasets such as ImageNet. Our experimental findings demonstrate that both locality—capturing fine-grained input elements—and compositionality—the ability to express representations through a compact vocabulary—are fundamentally linked to model generalization. These results underscore the importance of developing more locally-aware models as a promising direction for future research in representation learning.

input:
We consider training machine learning models that are fair in the sense that
their performance is invariant under certain sensitive perturbations to the
inputs. For example, the performance of a resume screening system should be
invariant under changes to the gender and/or ethnicity of the applicant. We
formalize this notion of algorithmic fairness as a variant of individual
fairness and develop a distributionally robust optimization approach to enforce
it during training. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach on
two ML tasks that are susceptible to gender and racial biases.
Improve this in GPT way: We propose training machine learning models to be fair by ensuring their performance remains consistent when specific sensitive attributes in the inputs are altered. For instance, a resume screening model should perform equally well regardless of changes to an applicant’s gender or ethnicity. We formalize this fairness concept as a form of individual fairness and introduce a distributionally robust optimization method to enforce it during training. The approach’s effectiveness is demonstrated on two machine learning tasks prone to gender and racial biases.

input:
Deep Reinforcement Learning (Deep RL) has been receiving increasingly more
attention thanks to its encouraging performance on a variety of control tasks.
Yet, conventional regularization techniques in training neural networks (e.g.,
$L_2$ regularization, dropout) have been largely ignored in RL methods,
possibly because agents are typically trained and evaluated in the same
environment, and because the deep RL community focuses more on high-level
algorithm designs. In this work, we present the first comprehensive study of
regularization techniques with multiple policy optimization algorithms on
continuous control tasks. Interestingly, we find conventional regularization
techniques on the policy networks can often bring large improvement, especially
on harder tasks. Our findings are shown to be robust against training
hyperparameter variations. We also compare these techniques with the more
widely used entropy regularization. In addition, we study regularizing
different components and find that only regularizing the policy network is
typically the best. We further analyze why regularization may help
generalization in RL from four perspectives - sample complexity, reward
distribution, weight norm, and noise robustness. We hope our study provides
guidance for future practices in regularizing policy optimization algorithms.
Our code is available at https://github.com/xuanlinli17/iclr2021_rlreg .
Improve this in GPT way: Deep Reinforcement Learning (Deep RL) has attracted growing attention due to its strong performance across diverse control tasks. However, conventional neural network regularization methods—such as \(L_2\) regularization and dropout—have been largely overlooked in RL. This may be because agents are usually trained and tested in the same environment, and because the community has prioritized high-level algorithmic innovations. In this work, we conduct the first comprehensive study of regularization techniques using multiple policy optimization algorithms on continuous control benchmarks. Notably, we show that applying standard regularization to policy networks often yields substantial gains, particularly on more difficult tasks. These results remain robust across variations in training hyperparameters. We also compare these approaches with the more common entropy regularization and demonstrate that regularizing only the policy network generally performs best. Furthermore, we analyze how regularization improves generalization in RL from four angles: sample complexity, reward distribution, weight norms, and robustness to noise. We hope this study offers practical guidance for integrating regularization into policy optimization algorithms. Our code is available at https://github.com/xuanlinli17/iclr2021_rlreg.

input:
We propose an algorithm combining calibrated prediction and generalization
bounds from learning theory to construct confidence sets for deep neural
networks with PAC guarantees---i.e., the confidence set for a given input
contains the true label with high probability. We demonstrate how our approach
can be used to construct PAC confidence sets on ResNet for ImageNet, a visual
object tracking model, and a dynamics model for the half-cheetah reinforcement
learning problem.
Improve this in GPT way: We introduce a method that merges calibrated prediction with learning-theoretic generalization bounds to build PAC-guaranteed confidence sets for deep neural networks. These sets contain the true label with high probability for any given input. We validate our approach by constructing such sets for a ResNet on ImageNet, a visual object tracker, and a dynamics model in a half-cheetah reinforcement learning task.

input:
We address the problem of graph classification based only on structural
information. Inspired by natural language processing techniques (NLP), our
model sequentially embeds information to estimate class membership
probabilities. Besides, we experiment with NLP-like variational regularization
techniques, making the model predict the next node in the sequence as it reads
it. We experimentally show that our model achieves state-of-the-art
classification results on several standard molecular datasets. Finally, we
perform a qualitative analysis and give some insights on whether the node
prediction helps the model better classify graphs.
Improve this in GPT way: We tackle graph classification using only structural data. Drawing inspiration from natural language processing (NLP), our approach sequentially embeds information to estimate class probabilities. We also incorporate NLP-style variational regularization, training the model to predict the next node while processing a sequence. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art classification performance on multiple benchmark molecular datasets. A qualitative analysis further explores whether this node prediction task enhances the model’s classification ability.

input:
In this paper, we introduce Symplectic ODE-Net (SymODEN), a deep learning
framework which can infer the dynamics of a physical system, given by an
ordinary differential equation (ODE), from observed state trajectories. To
achieve better generalization with fewer training samples, SymODEN incorporates
appropriate inductive bias by designing the associated computation graph in a
physics-informed manner. In particular, we enforce Hamiltonian dynamics with
control to learn the underlying dynamics in a transparent way, which can then
be leveraged to draw insight about relevant physical aspects of the system,
such as mass and potential energy. In addition, we propose a parametrization
which can enforce this Hamiltonian formalism even when the generalized
coordinate data is embedded in a high-dimensional space or we can only access
velocity data instead of generalized momentum. This framework, by offering
interpretable, physically-consistent models for physical systems, opens up new
possibilities for synthesizing model-based control strategies.
Improve this in GPT way: This paper presents Symplectic ODE-Net (SymODEN), a deep learning framework designed to infer the dynamics of a physical system—expressed as an ordinary differential equation (ODE)—from observed state trajectories. To enhance generalization with limited data, SymODEN incorporates physics-informed inductive bias by structuring its computation graph accordingly. Specifically, it enforces controlled Hamiltonian dynamics, enabling transparent learning of the underlying system. This approach yields interpretable models that reveal physical properties like mass and potential energy. Furthermore, we introduce a parametrization that preserves the Hamiltonian structure even when generalized coordinates are high-dimensional or only velocity data—rather than canonical momentum—is available. By providing physically consistent models, SymODEN creates new opportunities for developing model-based control strategies.

input:
Graph embedding techniques have been increasingly deployed in a multitude of
different applications that involve learning on non-Euclidean data. However,
existing graph embedding models either fail to incorporate node attribute
information during training or suffer from node attribute noise, which
compromises the accuracy. Moreover, very few of them scale to large graphs due
to their high computational complexity and memory usage. In this paper we
propose GraphZoom, a multi-level framework for improving both accuracy and
scalability of unsupervised graph embedding algorithms. GraphZoom first
performs graph fusion to generate a new graph that effectively encodes the
topology of the original graph and the node attribute information. This fused
graph is then repeatedly coarsened into much smaller graphs by merging nodes
with high spectral similarities. GraphZoom allows any existing embedding
methods to be applied to the coarsened graph, before it progressively refine
the embeddings obtained at the coarsest level to increasingly finer graphs. We
have evaluated our approach on a number of popular graph datasets for both
transductive and inductive tasks. Our experiments show that GraphZoom can
substantially increase the classification accuracy and significantly accelerate
the entire graph embedding process by up to 40.8x, when compared to the
state-of-the-art unsupervised embedding methods.
Improve this in GPT way:
Graph embedding methods are widely used for learning from non-Euclidean data, yet current approaches face significant limitations. Many models either ignore node attributes during training or are sensitive to noisy attributes, which reduces accuracy. Additionally, most techniques struggle with large-scale graphs due to high computational and memory demands. To address these issues, we introduce GraphZoom, a multi-level framework designed to enhance both the accuracy and scalability of unsupervised graph embeddings.

GraphZoom begins by fusing the original graph structure with node attributes, creating an enriched graph that captures both topological and feature information. This fused graph is then iteratively coarsened by merging spectrally similar nodes, producing progressively smaller graphs. Any existing embedding method can be applied efficiently to the coarsest graph. The framework subsequently refines the resulting embeddings through successive levels back to the original graph. Evaluated on multiple benchmark datasets for transductive and inductive tasks, GraphZoom significantly improves classification accuracy and accelerates the embedding process by up to 40.8× compared to state-of-the-art unsupervised methods.

input:
Distributed optimization is vital in solving large-scale machine learning
problems. A widely-shared feature of distributed optimization techniques is the
requirement that all nodes complete their assigned tasks in each computational
epoch before the system can proceed to the next epoch. In such settings, slow
nodes, called stragglers, can greatly slow progress. To mitigate the impact of
stragglers, we propose an online distributed optimization method called Anytime
Minibatch. In this approach, all nodes are given a fixed time to compute the
gradients of as many data samples as possible. The result is a variable
per-node minibatch size. Workers then get a fixed communication time to average
their minibatch gradients via several rounds of consensus, which are then used
to update primal variables via dual averaging. Anytime Minibatch prevents
stragglers from holding up the system without wasting the work that stragglers
can complete. We present a convergence analysis and analyze the wall time
performance. Our numerical results show that our approach is up to 1.5 times
faster in Amazon EC2 and it is up to five times faster when there is greater
variability in compute node performance.
Improve this in GPT way: Distributed optimization is essential for tackling large-scale machine learning tasks. A common limitation of these methods is their synchronous nature: every node must finish its work within each computational epoch before the system can advance. This makes overall progress highly vulnerable to delays from slower nodes, known as stragglers. To address this, we introduce Anytime Minibatch, an online distributed optimization technique. Instead of fixed workloads, each node computes gradients for as many data samples as possible within a fixed computation window, creating variable per-node minibatch sizes. Workers then use a fixed communication interval to average these gradients through multiple consensus rounds, followed by a primal update via dual averaging. This design prevents stragglers from blocking the system while still utilizing all completed work. We provide a convergence analysis and evaluate wall-clock performance. Empirical results on Amazon EC2 demonstrate speedups of up to 1.5 times under normal conditions, and up to five times faster when node performance variability is high.

input:
Scaling end-to-end reinforcement learning to control real robots from vision
presents a series of challenges, in particular in terms of sample efficiency.
Against end-to-end learning, state representation learning can help learn a
compact, efficient and relevant representation of states that speeds up policy
learning, reducing the number of samples needed, and that is easier to
interpret. We evaluate several state representation learning methods on goal
based robotics tasks and propose a new unsupervised model that stacks
representations and combines strengths of several of these approaches. This
method encodes all the relevant features, performs on par or better than
end-to-end learning with better sample efficiency, and is robust to
hyper-parameters change.
Improve this in GPT way: Training robots with end-to-end reinforcement learning directly from visual inputs remains challenging, primarily due to poor sample efficiency. As an alternative, state representation learning can extract a compact and interpretable low-dimensional encoding from raw pixels, which significantly accelerates policy training. We assess multiple such methods on goal-based robotic tasks and introduce a novel unsupervised model. By stacking and combining the strengths of existing approaches, our method captures all essential features, matches or surpasses end-to-end learning performance with superior sample efficiency, and maintains robustness to variations in hyper-parameters.

input:
A central challenge in reinforcement learning is discovering effective
policies for tasks where rewards are sparsely distributed. We postulate that in
the absence of useful reward signals, an effective exploration strategy should
seek out {\it decision states}. These states lie at critical junctions in the
state space from where the agent can transition to new, potentially unexplored
regions. We propose to learn about decision states from prior experience. By
training a goal-conditioned policy with an information bottleneck, we can
identify decision states by examining where the model actually leverages the
goal state. We find that this simple mechanism effectively identifies decision
states, even in partially observed settings. In effect, the model learns the
sensory cues that correlate with potential subgoals. In new environments, this
model can then identify novel subgoals for further exploration, guiding the

of the state space.
Improve this in GPT way:
A core challenge in reinforcement learning is learning effective policies when rewards are sparse. We argue that without useful reward signals, a robust exploration strategy should seek *decision states*—critical junctions in the state space from which an agent can transition into new, potentially unexplored regions. Our approach learns to identify these states from prior experience. By training a goal-conditioned policy with an information bottleneck, we can pinpoint decision states by observing where the model meaningfully uses the goal information. This simple method reliably uncovers decision states, even under partial observability, effectively learning sensory cues that signal potential subgoals. When deployed in new environments, the model can detect novel subgoals to drive exploration, guiding the agent through a sequence of decision states and into uncharted areas of the state space.

Multilingual machine translation, which translates multiple languages with a
single model, has attracted much attention due to its efficiency of offline
training and online serving. However, traditional multilingual translation
usually yields inferior accuracy compared with the counterpart using individual
models for each language pair, due to language diversity and model capacity
limitations. In this paper, we propose a distillation-based approach to boost
the accuracy of multilingual machine translation. Specifically, individual
models are first trained and regarded as teachers, and then the multilingual
model is trained to fit the training data and match the outputs of individual
models simultaneously through knowledge distillation. Experiments on IWSLT, WMT
and Ted talk translation datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.
Particularly, we show that one model is enough to handle multiple languages (up
to 44 languages in our experiment), with comparable or even better accuracy
than individual models.
Improve this in GPT way:
Multilingual machine translation—using a single model for many languages—is valued for its efficiency in both training and deployment. Yet, it often underperforms compared to dedicated models for each language pair, hampered by linguistic diversity and finite model capacity.

To address this, we introduce a knowledge distillation method to enhance multilingual translation accuracy. First, we train high-performance individual models as “teachers.” Then, we train the multilingual “student” model not only on standard data, but also to align its outputs with those of the teacher models through distillation.

Experiments across IWSLT, WMT, and TED talk datasets confirm our approach’s effectiveness. Notably, we demonstrate that a single model can manage numerous languages—up to 44 in our tests—achieving accuracy on par with, or even surpassing, that of individual dedicated models.

We introduce PyTorch Geometric, a library for deep learning on irregularly
structured input data such as graphs, point clouds and manifolds, built upon
PyTorch. In addition to general graph data structures and processing methods,
it contains a variety of recently published methods from the domains of
relational learning and 3D data processing. PyTorch Geometric achieves high
data throughput by leveraging sparse GPU acceleration, by providing dedicated
CUDA kernels and by introducing efficient mini-batch handling for input
examples of different size. In this work, we present the library in detail and
perform a comprehensive comparative study of the implemented methods in
homogeneous evaluation scenarios.
Improve this in GPT way: We present PyTorch Geometric, a deep learning library built on PyTorch for handling irregularly structured data like graphs, point clouds, and manifolds. It provides general graph data structures and processing tools, along with a collection of recent methods from relational learning and 3D data analysis. The library achieves high throughput via sparse GPU acceleration, custom CUDA kernels, and efficient mini-batch handling for variably sized inputs. This paper details the library’s design and offers a thorough comparative evaluation of the implemented methods under consistent experimental conditions.

Although variational autoencoders (VAEs) represent a widely influential deep
generative model, many aspects of the underlying energy function remain poorly
understood. In particular, it is commonly believed that Gaussian
encoder/decoder assumptions reduce the effectiveness of VAEs in generating
realistic samples. In this regard, we rigorously analyze the VAE objective,
differentiating situations where this belief is and is not actually true. We
then leverage the corresponding insights to develop a simple VAE enhancement
that requires no additional hyperparameters or sensitive tuning.
Quantitatively, this proposal produces crisp samples and stable FID scores that
are actually competitive with a variety of GAN models, all while retaining
desirable attributes of the original VAE architecture. A shorter version of
this work will appear in the ICLR 2019 conference proceedings (Dai and Wipf,
2019). The code for our model is available at https://github.com/daib13/
TwoStageVAE.
Improve this in GPT way:
While variational autoencoders (VAEs) are a foundational deep generative model, key properties of their energy function remain unclear. This work provides a rigorous analysis of the VAE objective, precisely delineating when this belief holds and when it does not. Building on these insights, we introduce a straightforward enhancement to the VAE framework that requires no new hyperparameters or delicate tuning. The resulting model generates sharp samples and achieves stable Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) scores competitive with several GAN variants, while preserving the VAE's inherent advantages. A condensed version is published in ICLR 2019 (Dai & Wipf, 2019). Code is available at: https://github.com/daib13/TwoStageVAE.
